San Bartolo Coyotepec's black pottery is especially beautiful when lit from the side. A soft sheen appears on the smooth surface of a vessel, while the pierced design casts a delicate shadow on the table. The village south of Oaxaca is famous for barro negro, a tradition of local earthenware and decorative ceramics. Pottery-making skills are passed down through families.

The different stages of the process are particularly fascinating to watch. Craftspeople shape clay by hand, cut patterns into it and polish the surface with simple tools, including quartz stones. The black colour develops through a special firing process in a traditional kiln with a restricted supply of air. Beside a finished vase, an unfinished piece looks completely different, revealing how much work lies behind the familiar word 'pottery'.

In the centre of the village stands the Oaxaca Museum of Popular Art, MEAPO. Its collection introduces visitors to the crafts of Coyotepec and other communities in the region. The trip will appeal to lovers of applied arts: here you can study the shapes, ask craftspeople questions and choose an object that will bring pleasure at home long after your travels.

San Bernardino is part of Paraguay's lakeside region. The town sits amid greenery, with lakeside walks and views of the water and hills. Travellers visit on routes from Asunción, combining a town stop with natural scenery.

The journey often continues to Areguá and farther into the Guairá region. San Bernardino offers an opportunity to linger beside the shore before exploring forest trails and waterfalls. Part of its appeal is the transition from the capital's urban neighbourhoods to a lakeside setting where water and green slopes dominate the scenery.

San Cristóbal introduces travellers to the Galápagos through the sea and island life. In Puerto Baquerizo Moreno, the archipelago's capital, you can stroll along the waterfront and watch sea lions. They have become some of the most recognisable inhabitants of the local coastline. Beyond the town, beaches, nature trails and green hills begin.

Off the coast stand the rocks of León Dormido, also known as Kicker Rock. Two tall rocky sections are separated by a narrow channel of seawater. From a boat, their sheer walls are clearly visible, while snorkelling excursions offer an introduction to the marine life of the area. The type of visit is chosen according to ocean conditions and participants' experience.

On the island itself, La Lobería, Punta Carola and the Tijeretas area are worth visiting. Here, walks along the shore go hand in hand with watching animals and birds. Sea lions are especially fascinating when observed from a distance: one rests on the beach, another emerges from the water, and an ordinary stretch of sand becomes a place to linger and watch.

The highlands of San Cristóbal reveal a different landscape. Among green hills lies El Junco, a freshwater lagoon inside the crater of an extinct volcano. A journey into the island's interior adds cool air and lush vegetation to the experiences of the coast. San Cristóbal is ideal for travellers who want to combine shoreline walks, wildlife encounters and boat trips, allowing time for each.

Stopping in San Cristóbal offers a glimpse of the inhabited side of the region. The exact activities during the visit are set out in the itinerary of the chosen trip.
